intro:
This track has two parts. Lessons 1 to 12 are the ideas that cross stores: the Bigtable and Dynamo papers, keys designed from access patterns, partitioning on a hash ring, replication with N, R and W, consistency and conflicts, and transactions, with one lead store per data model (DynamoDB, Cassandra, MongoDB, Neo4j) plus search, time-series and vector stores. Lessons 13 to 18 go inside each store and set it up: Cassandra's ring, gossip and failure detection and how to run a cluster, MongoDB replica sets and sharding, DynamoDB's partitions and capacity, Neo4j's storage and memory, and OpenSearch's shards and replicas. At the end you can design keys for a payments service in any of them, predict what a read sees while replicas disagree, and say what a cluster does when a node dies or one key runs hot.

You need to program, and nothing else. The database internals track explains the parts these stores are built from (B+trees, LSM trees, write-ahead logging, MVCC, Raft), the SQL track's isolation levels and recursive queries come back in lessons 9 to 11, and the second part borrows the page cache, fsync, mmap and cgroups from the OS track. Every lesson reminds you of what it borrows in a sentence.

The labs live in `labs/nosql`, in Kotlin. Thirteen are models in plain Kotlin that test in a second, all six labs of the second part among them; the other five run against real stores that Testcontainers starts (DynamoDB Local, MongoDB 9.0, Neo4j 2026.10) and need Docker. The Try-its use Compose files in `labs/env`, and the second part adds clusters: `cassandra-cluster.yml` gains a `grow` profile (a fourth node) and a `dc2` profile (a node in a second datacenter), `mongo-sharded.yml` runs a config server, two shards and a mongos, and `opensearch-cluster.yml` runs three nodes. Each needs about 2 to 4 GB of Docker memory, so run one at a time and stop it with `down -v`, adding `--profile grow --profile dc2` if you started those nodes. Run everything from the `labs` folder; `./gradlew :nosql:test --tests 'sfz.nosql.lNN.*'` runs one lesson's lab.
cheatsheet:
## Families: what you store decides what you can ask

| Family | You find data by | Lead store | Built in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Key-value | its key, or a sorted run in one partition | DynamoDB | lessons 3, 4, 16 |
| Wide-column | partition key, then a slice of clustering columns | Cassandra 5.0 | lessons 7, 13, 14 |
| Document | any indexed field of a JSON-like document | MongoDB 9.0 | lessons 8, 15 |
| Graph | a start node, then a walk along relationships | Neo4j 2026.10 | lessons 11, 17 |
| Search | words, through an inverted index, ranked by BM25 | OpenSearch 3.9 | lessons 12, 18 |
| Time-series | a time range, through chunks and rolled-up buckets | TimescaleDB 2.31 | lesson 12 |
| Vector | nearest neighbours of an embedding, through HNSW | pgvector 0.8.7 | lesson 12 |

Two placement answers sit under them (lesson 1): Bigtable sorts keys and cuts them into ranges; Dynamo hashes keys onto a ring and copies each to N nodes. Cassandra is Dynamo's ring with Bigtable's storage. DynamoDB is not Dynamo: each partition has a Multi-Paxos leader (lesson 16).

## Keys come from the questions (lessons 2, 3, 7)

- Write every access pattern down with its rate before choosing a key.
- Partition key: `=` on all its parts; it picks the partition (hashed). Sort key or clustering columns: sorted inside the partition; `=` on leading parts, then one range, no gaps.
- Every query is a key lookup, a range read or a scan. A filter runs after the read and pays for everything read.
- A question the key can't answer gets another copy: a GSI, another Cassandra table, another MongoDB index. Each copy costs a write on every insert, and a DynamoDB GSI lags and can't be read strongly consistently.

## Numbers worth remembering

| What | Value |
|---|---|
| DynamoDB per partition | 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes a second; read unit 4 KB, write unit 1 KB; about 10 GB of data |
| DynamoDB transaction | up to 100 items, 4 MB, two writes per item, client token remembered 10 min |
| Cassandra hints | kept for `max_hint_window`, 3 h |
| Cassandra tombstones | kept `gc_grace_seconds`, 10 days; warn at 1,000 per read, fail at 100,000 |
| MongoDB election | after `electionTimeoutMillis`, 10 s; typically done within 12 s |
| MongoDB transaction | 60 s default lifetime; needs a replica set |
| Cassandra LWT (Paxos v1) | 4 round trips per write; v2 needs 2 |
| BM25 defaults | k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 |
| pgvector HNSW defaults | m = 16, ef_construction = 64, ef_search = 40 |

## Replication and quorums (lessons 6, 8)

- Leader-based (DynamoDB, MongoDB): one copy orders writes; failover needs an election. Leaderless (Dynamo, Cassandra): every write goes to all N replicas, W must acknowledge, a read asks R.
- R + W > N: every read set overlaps every acknowledged write set. N = 3, QUORUM = 2.
- Catch-up: hinted handoff (short outages), read repair (keys that get read), anti-entropy with Merkle trees (everything else).
- `Unavailable`: too few replicas alive, nothing tried. `WriteTimeout` or a `wtimeout`: tried, outcome unknown, may have landed.
- MongoDB `w: 1` can be rolled back after a failover; `w: "majority"`, the default since 5.0, survives it.

## Consistency and conflicts (lesson 9)

- Ladder: linearizable, sequential, causal, session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads), eventual.
- CAP: during a partition, a replica answers (A) or refuses (C). PACELC: else, latency or consistency, every day.
- Last write wins keeps one concurrent write and drops the other by clock. Vector clocks detect concurrency and return siblings. CRDTs merge in any order (G-Counter: max per slot; OR-Set: remove the tags you saw).

## Transactions (lessons 4, 10)

- Across partitions: every participant promises (prepare), one decision is recorded durably, then commit. That's two-phase commit.
- DynamoDB: a rejected prepare is `TransactionConflict`; nothing waits; retry with backoff and the same idempotency key.
- MongoDB: snapshot per transaction; first writer wins; `TransientTransactionError` means rerun the whole transaction; set `snapshot` and `majority`.
- Cassandra LWT: Paxos on one partition (prepare, read, propose, commit), `[applied]` in the reply. Accord in 6.0 (alpha): `BEGIN TRANSACTION` across partitions.
- Prefer one document, one conditional write, or a saga of single-partition steps when the business can see "pending".

## Graphs and specialized stores (lessons 11, 12)

- Cypher: `MATCH (a:Account {id: $id})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(b)`; repeat with `((...)){1,3}`; `-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}` for cycles. Start from an index, bound every walk, keep supernodes out.
- Search: analyzer, posting lists, BM25. Time-series: chunks, `time_bucket`, keep count and sum, drop old chunks. Vectors: exact is a full comparison; HNSW walks layers with a beam of `ef_search`; measure recall@k.
- Every extra store is a copy: feed it from an outbox through Kafka, never by dual writes, and watch its lag.

## Inside each store (lessons 13 to 18)

### Cassandra: the ring, gossip and failure detection (lesson 13)

There is no master. Every node keeps the whole map (each node's tokens, datacenter, rack, state, load and schema version), saves it in `system.local` and `system.peers_v2`, and works out a key's replicas by itself.

- Murmur3 turns a partition key into a 64-bit token, every node owns 16 tokens, and a key's copies go to the owners of the next tokens clockwise. The allocator (`allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3`) places a joining node's tokens to within about 2% of even. A node picks its tokens once, at its first start.

| Replication strategy | Where the copies go | Use it |
|---|---|---|
| `SimpleStrategy` | the first RF distinct nodes clockwise; racks and datacenters ignored | never in production, system keyspaces included (`system_auth` starts with 1 copy) |
| `NetworkTopologyStrategy` | RF per datacenter (`{'dc1': 3, 'dc2': 3}`), one copy per rack; a rack repeats only when a datacenter has fewer racks than copies | always, with 3 racks of equal size per datacenter |

| Snitch | What it does |
|---|---|
| `SimpleSnitch` (the default) | puts every node in `datacenter1` and `rack1` |
| `GossipingPropertyFileSnitch` | reads the node's `dc` and `rack` from `cassandra-rackdc.properties` and gossips them; the production choice |
| dynamic snitch | wraps the snitch and re-ranks replicas for reads by measured latency every 100 ms |

Choose the snitch, datacenters and racks before the first write. Switching to an incompatible snitch once data is in the cluster loses data.

Gossip: every second, each node starts one exchange with a random peer, and now and then with a seed too.

| Message | Carries |
|---|---|
| GossipDigestSyn | one digest per known node: endpoint, generation, highest version |
| GossipDigestAck | the states the receiver has that are newer, plus requests for the ones that are newer at the sender |
| GossipDigestAck2 | the requested states |

- A version is one counter per node, bumped by every heartbeat and every change to its own state. The generation is the node's start time in seconds. Generations are compared first, so a restarted node's new, small versions still replace its old life.
- News reaches N nodes in about log2 N rounds: a median of 2 rounds for 6 nodes, 8 for 6,000. Schema travels as a UUID, and `nodetool describecluster` should list one version.
- Seeds are first contacts for a starting node and extra gossip partners, never masters. Use two or three stable nodes per datacenter, the same list on every node. A seed never bootstraps, so a new node must not list itself.

Phi accrual failure detection:

- phi = silence / (mean gap × ln 10), about 0.434 × t / m, over the last 1,000 gaps between newer heartbeats. Gaps longer than 2 s are never recorded.
- `phi_convict_threshold` is 8 by default; leave it. Phi passes 8 after 18.4 mean gaps: about 18 to 20 s with 1 s gaps, about 28 s with 1.5 s gaps. A node that was itself paused for more than 5 s marks nobody down.
- DOWN is each node's own decision and is never gossiped. A clean shutdown is announced, so peers mark it down within a second. Down means hints (for up to `max_hint_window`, 3 h) and no reads, never removal from the ring.

A coordinator hashes the key, walks its own ring, and counts live replicas against the consistency level (too few: `Unavailable`, nothing sent). It sends the write to every live replica, keeps a hint for the rest, and answers after enough acknowledgements (`WriteTimeout` after `write_request_timeout`, 2 s in the lab). The Java driver sends prepared statements straight to a replica (token-aware routing).

### Setting up and running Cassandra (lesson 14)

A node is one JVM plus four directories: `commitlog/` (32 MiB segments), `data/` (SSTables, and later `snapshots/` and `backups/`), `hints/` and `saved_caches/`. Set the heap yourself (`MAX_HEAP_SIZE`), because the default reads the host's RAM, not the container's limit, and leave the rest of the RAM to the page cache.

| `cassandra.yaml` setting | Decides | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| `cluster_name` | which cluster the node joins | gossip drops other names; saved at first start |
| `seeds` (under `seed_provider`) | first contacts | 2 or 3 per datacenter, never a joining node |
| `listen_address`, `broadcast_address` | the address other nodes use, port 7000 | never 0.0.0.0 |
| `rpc_address`, `broadcast_rpc_address` | the address clients use, port 9042 | 0.0.0.0 needs `broadcast_rpc_address` |
| `endpoint_snitch` | datacenter and rack | `GossipingPropertyFileSnitch` |
| `num_tokens`, `allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor` | how many tokens, and where | 16 (4 past about 30 nodes) and your RF; first start only |
| `commitlog_sync: periodic`, `commitlog_sync_period: 10000ms` | when the commit log is fsynced | the node acks before the fsync, so one machine can lose 10 s; the other replicas still have it |
| `data_file_directories`, `commitlog_directory`, `hints_directory`, `saved_caches_directory` | where the files go | under `/var/lib/cassandra` in the image |
| `auto_bootstrap: false` | join without streaming | only for a new datacenter, followed by `rebuild` |

Keyspaces use `NetworkTopologyStrategy` with the datacenter names the snitch reports, letter for letter. Alter `system_auth`, `system_distributed` and `system_traces` to match, then repair them.

| `nodetool` command | When to use it |
|---|---|
| `status` | first look: `UN` everywhere, or a `DN`, `UJ` or `UL` that shouldn't be there |
| `describecluster` | one schema version? which keyspaces replicate how |
| `info` | heap, generation, datacenter and rack, bootstrap state |
| `gossipinfo` | the node's whole map: generation, heartbeat and the versioned states |
| `failuredetector` | phi for every peer |
| `getendpoints <ks> <table> <key>`, `describering <ks>` | which nodes hold a key; every range with its replicas |
| `tablestats <ks.table>` | SSTable count, latency, tombstones per slice, largest partition against 100 MB |
| `compactionstats` | pending compactions; a number that keeps growing means compaction is falling behind |
| `tpstats` | pending and blocked thread pools, dropped messages |
| `cleanup` | on each old node, one at a time, after the last new node is `UN` |
| `repair` (incremental), `repair --full`, `-pr`, `--preview` | incremental every 1 to 3 days, full every 1 to 3 weeks, every node within `gc_grace_seconds` (10 days); `-pr` on every node; `--preview` shows what would stream |
| `drain` | before every restart: stops client traffic, announces the shutdown, flushes the memtables |
| `decommission` | on a live node that is leaving: it streams its own ranges away |
| `removenode <host ID>` | on any live node, for a dead one: the survivors stream; repair after |
| `rebuild -- dc1` | on each node of a new datacenter, after `ALTER KEYSPACE` |
| `snapshot`, `clearsnapshot`, `enablebackup` | hard-linked backups: copy them off the node, then clear them |

- A joining node learns the map and schema from a seed, picks its tokens and gossips them (`UJ`, and from now on it gets new writes for its ranges), sleeps `ring_delay` (30 s), streams each range from the replica it replaces, then shows `UN`. One join at a time. The old nodes keep their copies until `cleanup`.
- A dead node's machine is gone: start the new one with `-Dcassandra.replace_address_first_boot=<dead address>` and it takes over the tokens and streams their data.
- To add a datacenter, start its nodes with `dc=dc2` and `auto_bootstrap: false`, add `dc2` with `ALTER KEYSPACE`, run `nodetool rebuild -- dc1` on each, and only then send the region's clients there with `LOCAL_QUORUM`. Before the rebuild, `LOCAL_*` reads come back empty, with no error.

### MongoDB: replica sets, sharding and the balancer (lesson 15)

- `mongod` keeps each collection and index as a WiredTiger B-tree file. The cache is the larger of 50% of (RAM minus 1 GB) and 256 MB; a checkpoint runs every 60 s, with a journal between checkpoints.
- The oplog (`local.oplog.rs`) is a capped collection of idempotent entries: the result (`amountMinor: 4350`), not the `$inc`. Default size 5% of free disk, 990 MB to 50 GB. Its window is how long a member may be away before it needs a full initial sync.
- Members send heartbeats every 2 s. After `electionTimeoutMillis` (10 s) without the primary, a secondary raises the term and asks for votes; each member votes once per term, only for a candidate whose oplog is at least as recent; a majority of voters wins. Up to 50 members, 7 voting. `priority` picks the preferred primary (0: never), `hidden` and `secondaryDelaySecs` do side jobs. Avoid arbiters: in a primary, secondary and arbiter set, losing the secondary stalls `w: "majority"` writes.

| Sharded cluster part | Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| shard | part of every sharded collection | a replica set, three members in production |
| config server replica set | the `config` database: `config.shards`, `config.collections`, `config.chunks` | the balancer runs on its primary; no arbiters or delayed members; without a primary nothing moves |
| `mongos` | nothing on disk, only a cached chunk map | applications connect only here; run several; after a `StaleConfig` reply it refreshes and retries |

| Shard key rule | Why |
|---|---|
| many distinct values | all documents with one value share one chunk: `currency` can never use more than 3 shards |
| no dominant value | M-0042's fifth of the payments becomes a jumbo chunk that can't split or move |
| no steady growth | `createdAt`, or an `ObjectId` `_id`, sends every insert to the chunk ending at MaxKey, on one shard |
| in the busiest queries | with the key, `explain()` says `SINGLE_SHARD`; without it the query scatters to every shard (`SHARD_MERGE`) |
| the prefix of every unique index | only then is uniqueness enforced across the cluster; even `_id` is unique only per shard otherwise |

Ranged sharding keeps neighbours together, so a range of the key is targeted. Hashed sharding spreads a growing key evenly but targets only an equality. For payments, `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }` spreads accounts and keeps one account's payments together in time order.

Chunks are 128 MB by default, and since 6.0.3 inserts never split them. The balancer moves about one chunk size when the shards holding the most and the least of a collection differ by 3 chunk sizes (384 MB), one migration per shard at a time, while writes continue. The donor's old copies stay as orphans until it deletes them.

| Command | When |
|---|---|
| `rs.initiate({ _id: "rs0", members: [...] })` | once, on one member, to form the set |
| `rs.conf()`, `rs.status()`, `rs.stepDown(20, 5)` | members and priorities; term and states; a planned failover |
| `rs.printReplicationInfo()`, `rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo()` | oplog size and window; replication lag |
| `replSetResizeOplog`, `oplogMinRetentionHours` | a bigger window, or a floor in hours |
| `mongod --shardsvr`, `mongod --configsvr`, `mongos --configdb cfg/cfg1:27017` | start the parts |
| `sh.addShard("shard1/shard1:27017")` | once per shard, on mongos |
| `sh.shardCollection("sfz.payments", { _id: "hashed" })` | shard a collection (no `sh.enableSharding()` needed since 6.0) |
| `sh.status()`, `db.payments.getShardDistribution()`, `sh.balancerCollectionStatus()` | the chunks; data per shard; balanced or not |
| `analyzeShardKey` (7.0 and later) | score a candidate key from sampled queries |
| `refineCollectionShardKey` | add suffix fields so a jumbo chunk can split |
| `reshardCollection` (5.0 and later) | a new key: a full copy, so plan it like a migration |
| `sh.addShardToZone`, `sh.updateZoneKeyRange` | pin key ranges to shards, such as EU accounts on EU hardware |
| the balancer's `activeWindow` | keep migrations out of peak hours |

### DynamoDB under the hood (lesson 16)

A request router authenticates the request (with cached IAM results), takes tokens from the table's budget, hashes the partition key and finds its partition in a map cached from MemDS. A partition is three replicas in three availability zones, a Multi-Paxos group whose leader holds a lease. The leader takes writes and strongly consistent reads and acknowledges once 2 of 3 have the log record; an eventually consistent read can come from any replica. After a leader dies, the new one waits out the old lease, a couple of seconds.

| Partitions | Rule |
|---|---|
| ceiling per partition | 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU and about 10 GB |
| splits | near 10 GB, when provisioned throughput needs more partitions, and for consumption at a key chosen from the traffic; partitions never merge |
| what a split can't help | one hot item; a key range written in order (one partition key with a timestamp sort key) |
| a provisioned example | 3,200 WCU: 4 partitions of 800; raised to 6,000: 8 of 750; lowered to 5,000: still 8, of 625 |

| Capacity mode | How it behaves | Choose it for |
|---|---|---|
| provisioned: RCU and WCU, auto scaling, paid by the hour | burst: a partition spends up to 300 s of its saved unused share; adaptive capacity: a throttled partition gets the table's unused units, up to 1,000 WCU; global admission control: routers keep token buckets refilled from a central service | steady load you can forecast; cheaper per unit |
| on-demand (`PAY_PER_REQUEST`): paid per request | a new table takes 4,000 writes and 12,000 reads a second, then up to double its previous peak at once; past double within 30 minutes it can throttle; capped by a per-table quota (40,000 units by default) or your own lower maximum; pre-warm with warm throughput | new, spiky or unforecastable traffic |

A table can switch to on-demand four times in 24 hours, and back at any time.

A throttle is HTTP 400 with nothing changed. The SDK retries with backoff, so you see latency first and an exception later, and `ThrottlingReasons` names the limit:

| Reason | Means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded` | one partition's ceiling: a hot key | spread the key (lesson 5's write sharding); more capacity changes nothing |
| `TableWriteProvisionedThroughputExceeded` | the table's provisioned capacity | raise it, or switch to on-demand |
| `IndexWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded` | a GSI can't absorb the updates, so base-table writes are held back | give every GSI at least the table's write capacity and a key as good as the table's |

DynamoDB Local models no partitions, splits, throttling or point-in-time recovery, so test throttling against the lab's model or a real table.

After the partition commits, the copies follow on their own: GSIs lag and answer only eventually consistent reads, Streams keep each change 24 hours in order per item, TTL deletes within a few days without write units, point-in-time recovery keeps 1 to 35 days, and global tables run as MREC (last writer wins) or MRSC (GA June 2025, exactly three Regions, zero RPO, chosen at creation).

### Neo4j: records, memory and editions (lesson 17)

| Record | Bytes | Holds |
|---|---|---|
| node | 15 | in-use flag, first relationship, first property record, labels |
| relationship | 34 | its two nodes, its type, previous and next in each node's chain, first property record |
| property | 41 | four 8-byte blocks, so small values fit inline |

Record N starts at byte N × size, so a hop is a multiplication and a read, whatever the size of the graph. Files move in 8 KB pages (in the `aligned` format, 546 node or 240 relationship records each). A node's relationships form a doubly linked chain, newest first, and the head stores the degree. Past 50 relationships (`db.relationship_grouping_threshold`) a node gets one chain per type and direction. Indexes only find where a walk starts.

| | Page cache | Heap |
|---|---|---|
| holds | store files and native indexes in 8 KB pages, off-heap | query plans, rows in flight, uncommitted transaction state |
| setting | `server.memory.pagecache.size` | `server.memory.heap.initial_size` equal to `server.memory.heap.max_size` |
| size | store plus indexes plus 20% (a 35 GB store gets 42 GB) | enough for the concurrent work, at most 31 GB |

Leave the operating system at least 1 GB, more for full-text and vector indexes, and start from `neo4j-admin server memory-recommendation`. A commit is appended to the transaction log and fsynced, then applied in the page cache. A checkpoint (every 15 minutes or 100,000 transactions, and on shutdown) writes dirty pages to the store files, and recovery replays the log from there after a crash.

| | Community | Enterprise |
|---|---|---|
| servers | one standalone server | clusters: primaries commit on a Raft majority (2F + 1 survive F failures, at most 11), secondaries pull the log and serve reads (up to 20) |
| databases | `system` and one user database; `CREATE DATABASE` fails | several, each with its own topology (`CREATE DATABASE ... TOPOLOGY 3 PRIMARIES 2 SECONDARIES`) |
| backup | offline: stop the server, `neo4j-admin database dump`, restore with `load` | online `backup` and `restore`, full and differential |
| store format | `aligned` | `block`, the default for new databases since 5.22 |

A `neo4j://` driver fetches a routing table (TTL 300 s) and sends each write transaction to the writer; `bolt://` talks to one server only.

### OpenSearch: nodes, shards and replicas (lesson 18)

| Node role | Does |
|---|---|
| `cluster_manager` | may be elected cluster manager, and votes |
| `data` | holds shards: indexes documents and runs searches |
| `ingest` | runs ingest pipelines before indexing |
| coordinating (every node; `node.roles: []` for only this) | takes a request, sends it to the shards, merges the answers |

Production clusters usually run three dedicated cluster managers and separate data nodes. The elected cluster manager is the only node that changes the cluster state (nodes, mappings, the routing table). It wins by a majority of the voting nodes, so you need three eligible ones. `discovery.seed_hosts` finds the peers; `cluster.initial_cluster_manager_nodes` is read only when the cluster forms for the first time.

- A document's shard is `hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards`, with `_routing` = `_id` by default (a 3-shard index really has 768 routing slots). The primary count is fixed at creation: reindex, or `_split` into a multiple.
- Replicas are full copies on other nodes, never next to another copy of their shard. They serve searches, get promoted when a primary's node dies, and `number_of_replicas` can change at any time. An index with no settings gets 1 primary and 1 replica.
- A write goes to the primary (buffer plus translog, fsynced), then to every in-sync replica, then the ack. It's searchable after the next refresh (1 s); a `GET` by id is real-time.
- A search asks one copy of every shard for the ids and scores of its top `from + size`, merges them, then fetches only the page. `index.max_result_window` is 10,000; page deeper with `search_after`.

| Health | Means |
|---|---|
| green | every primary and every replica is assigned |
| yellow | every primary is assigned, some replica isn't: all data searchable, less redundancy |
| red | some primary is unassigned: some documents can't be searched, and writes to that shard fail |

When a node leaves, the manager removes it after 3 missed checks a second apart and promotes replicas for its primaries. The missing copies wait 1 minute (`index.unassigned.node_left.delayed_timeout`), then peer recovery rebuilds them at up to 40 MB a second per node.

| Sizing | Rule |
|---|---|
| shards | 10 to 50 GB each; at most 1,000 shard copies per node (`cluster.max_shards_per_node`); roll growing data over to a new index per day or week |
| heap | `-Xms` equal to `-Xmx`, half the RAM, at most about 31 GB; the other half feeds the page cache |
| operating system | `vm.max_map_count` at least 262,144; swap off |
| disk | 85% full: no new shards; 90%: shards move away; 95%: indices go read-only |
| security | TLS on HTTP and between nodes, plus users and roles (the lab switches it off) |

## Pairs people mix up

| This | Is not | The difference |
|---|---|---|
| CAP | PACELC | CAP is only about a network partition; PACELC adds the latency or consistency trade on normal days |
| Quorum (R + W > N) | Consensus (Paxos, Raft) | a quorum makes reads overlap writes; consensus makes replicas agree on one order or one value |
| Last write wins | Vector clocks | LWW silently keeps the later timestamp; vector clocks notice concurrent writes and hand both back |
| Embed | Reference | embed what is read and changed together and bounded; reference what grows without limit |
| Partition key | Clustering column | the partition key picks the machine and needs `=`; clustering columns order rows inside it and allow one range |
| Base table read | GSI read | the table can be read strongly consistently; a GSI lags and can't be |
| `Unavailable` | `WriteTimeout` | not attempted, against attempted with an unknown outcome |
| Lightweight transaction | Accord transaction | one partition, Paxos, Cassandra 5.0; many partitions and tables, 6.0 alpha |
| Exact nearest neighbours | Approximate (HNSW) | always right and reads everything; reads a little and may miss a neighbour |
| Seed | Master | a seed is a first contact for a starting node and an extra gossip partner; no Cassandra node is in charge |
| Gossip | Consensus | gossip spreads versioned state until every node has the same map, and nobody votes; consensus elects one leader by majority (MongoDB, Neo4j primaries, OpenSearch's cluster manager) |
| `SimpleStrategy` | `NetworkTopologyStrategy` | the first RF nodes on the ring, racks ignored; RF per datacenter and one copy per rack |
| `nodetool decommission` | `nodetool removenode` | the leaving node is alive and streams its own data; it's dead and the survivors stream |
| Ranged shard key | Hashed shard key | ranges stay targeted but a growing key puts every insert on one shard; inserts spread but a range asks every shard |
| Adaptive capacity | A hot key | lends a hot partition the table's spare units, up to 1,000 WCU; one key above that stays throttled until you spread it |
| Neo4j page cache | Neo4j heap | the store's pages, off-heap, sized to the store plus 20%; queries and transaction state, at most 31 GB |
| Primary shard | Replica shard | takes each write first, and its count is fixed at creation; a full copy on another node that serves searches and takes over, and its count changes any time |
recap: Bigtable sorts keys into ranges, and Dynamo hashes them onto a ring and copies each to N nodes; nearly every NoSQL store uses one, the other or both. Virtual nodes spread keys evenly and move few of them when nodes join, but they balance keys, not requests: a hot key needs write sharding or a cache.

Design keys from the access patterns: the partition key picks the partition and needs `=`, the sort key or clustering columns give cheap slices, and a question the key can't answer needs another copy of the data, which costs a write and may lag.

Leaderless replicas agree only as far as R + W > N makes reads and writes overlap. Hints, read repair and Merkle-tree repair converge them, and a timeout means "unknown", not "failed". Cassandra appends cells and writes deletes as tombstones; MongoDB writes one document atomically, and `w: "majority"` is what survives a failover.

Name the consistency you need per piece of data: CAP covers partitions, PACELC the daily latency trade, last write wins drops a concurrent write, vector clocks detect it and CRDTs merge it. Transactions exist in every store now, at a price (prepare and commit across partitions, conflicts and retries, four Paxos round trips), and a better data model often removes the need.

Graph stores walk relationships from an indexed start node; search, time-series and vector stores each build one index shaped like one question. Each extra store is a copy to feed from a log and to operate.

A Cassandra cluster has no master: every node keeps the whole map, gossip with one random peer a second keeps the copies in step, each node's phi detector decides by itself when a peer is down, and seeds are only first contacts. Set `cluster_name`, the snitch, racks and tokens before the first start, run `nodetool cleanup` after adding nodes, repair every node within `gc_grace_seconds` and drain before every restart.

A MongoDB replica set replays one elected primary's idempotent oplog, and the oplog window is how long a member may be away. Sharding adds a config server replica set that holds the chunk map and runs the balancer, and stateless mongos routers. The shard key decides where inserts land: a growing key puts all of them on one shard, a hashed key spreads them but scatters ranges.

DynamoDB kept Dynamo's name, not its design: a router sends each request to a partition of three replicas with a Multi-Paxos leader, and a partition takes at most 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU and about 10 GB. Partitions split and never merge. Adaptive capacity lends a hot partition the table's spare units only up to that ceiling, so one hot key stays throttled until you spread it.

Neo4j stores fixed-size records (nodes 15 bytes, relationships 34), so a hop is a multiplication and a read whatever the graph's size, and indexes only find where a walk starts. Size the page cache to the store plus 20% and keep the heap at 31 GB or less. Community is one server you back up offline; Enterprise adds online backups and Raft clusters of primaries and secondaries.

An OpenSearch index has a fixed number of primary shards, because routing divides a hash by that number, and replicas you can add at any time, never on the same node as another copy of their shard. One elected cluster manager changes the map. Losing a node turns health yellow until replicas are rebuilt; red means every copy of some shard is gone. Aim for shards of 10 to 50 GB.

quiz.q: A Cassandra table has `PRIMARY KEY ((account_id), created_at, payment_id)`. Which query does Cassandra refuse without `ALLOW FILTERING`?
options: `WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND created_at > '2026-11-01'`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' LIMIT 20`
`WHERE created_at > '2026-11-01'`
`WHERE account_id = 'A-1001' AND created_at = '2026-11-07 09:00' AND payment_id = 'pay-81723'`
quiz.why: The partition key, `account_id`, picks the machine and must be given with `=`; without it Cassandra would have to read every partition on every node. Clustering columns only order rows inside a partition, so a range on `created_at` is cheap once the partition is known (lessons 2 and 7).

quiz.q: A payment create must run once per idempotency key, even when two retries arrive together. In DynamoDB, what is the smallest tool that makes it safe?
options: A `TransactWriteItems` with the claim and nothing else
A GetItem to check for the key, then a PutItem if it's absent
One PutItem of the claim with `attribute_not_exists(pk)`
A strongly consistent read before the write
quiz.why: A condition expression makes the check and the write one atomic step on one item (lesson 3), and a second claim fails with `ConditionalCheckFailedException`. A read followed by a write races, whatever the read's consistency. A transaction works but costs two writes per item; you need one when the claim and the payment must be written together (lesson 4).

quiz.q: A provisioned DynamoDB table has 40,000 WCU and uses 6,000. Every payment also adds to one running-total item, `MERCH#M-0042#TOTAL`, 1,500 times a second, and about a third of those updates fail with `TableWriteKeyRangeThroughputExceeded`. What fixes it?
options: Raise the table to 80,000 WCU, so adaptive capacity has more spare units to lend
Switch the table to on-demand, which has no per-partition ceiling
Nothing: DynamoDB will split the hot partition for consumption within minutes
Spread the total over ten keys, `MERCH#M-0042#0` to `#9`, and add them up on read
quiz.why: Adaptive capacity lends a hot partition the table's unused units, but only up to the partition ceiling of 1,000 WCU, and this table already has 34,000 to spare (lesson 16). A split can't help either: one item has one key, so it lives in one partition, and the paper says such a partition won't benefit from a split. On-demand tables have the same partition ceilings. The reason says it too: `KeyRange` means one partition's limit, not the table's capacity. Lesson 5's write sharding turns one key into ten that hash to different places, so splits can put them on different partitions, each with its own 1,000 WCU.

quiz.q: Cassandra, N = 3, every read and write at `QUORUM`. Two requests claim the same idempotency key at the same moment with plain inserts. What does the quorum guarantee, and what does it not?
options: It guarantees only one insert succeeds
It guarantees reads overlap acknowledged writes, but both inserts succeed and last write wins keeps one silently; agreement on one winner needs Paxos (a lightweight transaction)
It guarantees nothing, because QUORUM is eventual consistency
It guarantees both claims are kept as siblings
quiz.why: A quorum is an overlap guarantee (lesson 6): any read of 2 sees any acknowledged write of 2. It doesn't order two writers. Consensus does: an LWT's Paxos rounds make replicas agree on one value before anyone writes (lesson 10). Siblings are Dynamo's, not Cassandra's.

quiz.q: A six-node Cassandra cluster has one seed, cass1, and cass1's machine is down for a day. In the same hour, the primary of a three-member MongoDB replica set dies. What happens in each?
options: Cassandra keeps serving reads and writes, but a brand-new node can't join until a seed is back; MongoDB's secondaries hold an election, and the one that wins a majority in the new term becomes primary
Both elect a replacement by majority vote, within about 12 seconds
Cassandra keeps serving, but no node can be marked down, because the seed collected the heartbeats; MongoDB's secondaries hold an election
Cassandra stops taking writes until the other nodes choose a new seed; MongoDB waits for the old primary, because only it holds the oplog
quiz.why: Cassandra keeps the Dynamo paper's symmetry: every node has the same job (lessons 1 and 13). Each node holds its own copy of the map, gossip keeps the copies in step, and each node's own failure detector decides who is down, so nothing waits for cass1. Gossip spreads state and nobody votes. A seed is only a first contact for a starting node and an extra gossip partner, which is why lesson 14 asks for two or three per datacenter. MongoDB's primary is chosen by consensus: after 10 seconds of silence a secondary raises the term and asks for votes, and 2 of 3 make it primary (lesson 15). Neo4j's primaries and OpenSearch's cluster managers use the same majority rule (lessons 17 and 18).

quiz.q: In MongoDB, should a payment's refunds be embedded in the payment, and an account's payments embedded in the account?
options: Embed both: one document per account is fastest
Reference both: documents should stay small
Embed the refunds (read and changed with the payment, a handful at most); reference the payments (they grow without limit)
Reference the refunds; embed the payments
quiz.why: Embed what is read and changed together and stays bounded: one guarded update can then check the refund rule atomically (lessons 2 and 8). An account's payments grow without limit and would run into the 16 MB document limit and rewrite a huge document on every payment, so they get their own collection, with at most a capped summary embedded.

quiz.q: A ledger collection is sharded on `{ createdAt: 1 }` so the month-end report reads a time range from few shards. `sh.status()` shows the data balanced, yet one shard's primary takes every insert. What explains it, and what would a hashed key trade?
options: The balancer is behind; once it finishes, new inserts spread over all the shards
The chunks are too big; with a smaller chunk size, inserts split the hot chunk across shards
Hashing `createdAt` instead would keep both: spread inserts and targeted time ranges

Every new `createdAt` is beyond all the others, so every insert lands in the chunk ending at MaxKey; a key like `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }` spreads inserts, but a time range over all accounts then asks every shard
quiz.why: Ranged sharding keeps neighbours together, so a time range is targeted, but a growing key sends every insert to the last chunk, on one shard (lesson 15). The balancer moves stored ranges, not the place the next insert goes, and since 6.0.3 inserts never split a chunk. Hashed sharding cuts the hash of the value, which spreads a growing key evenly, but only an equality on the hashed field stays targeted: neighbours hash far apart, so a range scatters. `{ accountId: "hashed", createdAt: 1 }` has the shape of lesson 7's Cassandra key and lesson 3's DynamoDB key: a hashed part that picks the place, then a sorted part inside it.

quiz.q: During a partition, one region voids a payment while the other captures it. Which conflict rule notices that the two writes were concurrent instead of silently keeping one?
options: Vector clocks: neither version's clock is behind the other's, so both are kept as siblings for the application
Last write wins with synchronized clocks
A quorum read at `ALL`
Read repair
quiz.why: Last write wins keeps the higher timestamp and drops the other write without a trace, and with skewed clocks the earlier decision can win (lesson 9). Vector clocks compare per-node counters: when each is ahead somewhere, the writes are concurrent and both come back. For payment status, the better answer is to stop the second write before it happens, with a single leader or a transaction (lesson 10).

quiz.q: The fraud team asks for accounts within three shared devices of a flagged account; support asks for disputes "like this one"; finance asks for merchants named like "Nrthwind". Which stores fit, in that order?
options: Search, graph, vector
Graph, vector, search
Vector, search, graph
Key-value for all three, with more indexes
quiz.why: A walk along shared identifiers is a graph question (lesson 11). Similar meaning is nearest neighbours of embeddings, a vector index (lesson 12). Typo-tolerant word matching ranked by relevance is an inverted index with fuzzy matching, a search engine (lesson 12). Each one can start inside a store you already run (pgvector, PostgreSQL full-text search) before you add a new one.

quiz.q: The disputes index on a three-node OpenSearch cluster has 3 primary shards and 1 replica. A teammate wants to change it in place to 6 primaries and 2 replicas. What happens?
options: The replica count changes at once and each shard gets a third copy, filled from its primary's segments; the primary count can't change in place, because each document's shard is `hash(_routing) % number_of_primary_shards`, so you `_split` 3 into 6 or reindex
Both change in place; OpenSearch moves documents into the new primaries in the background
The primary count changes in place, since a new primary is just a promoted replica; the replica count is fixed at creation
Neither changes in place; any change to an index's shards needs a reindex
quiz.why: Primaries and replicas hold the same documents but do different jobs (lesson 18). A write goes to the primary first and then to every in-sync replica, a search uses one copy of each shard, and a replica is promoted when its primary's node dies. `number_of_replicas` is a setting you can change any time, and each new copy fills itself by peer recovery. The primary count is the divisor in routing: change it and most documents hash to a different shard, the way lesson 5's `hash mod S` moved 80% of the keys. `_split` works only into a multiple, because each shard's range of routing slots cuts cleanly in two.
